# Training on the DGX Spark

GoverningDocs models train on the DGX Spark (ASUS Ascent GX10, GB10 GPU, 128 GB unified memory),
not on Colab or the laptop. Epic: [#19](https://github.com/governingdocs/data/issues/19).

The box is shared with a fine-tuning research programme, documented in `~/localrig` on the Mac.
**`~/localrig/OPERATING.md` (on the Mac) is the source of truth for operating the box**; this page covers only what GoverningDocs adds on top. Read its "Process and job control"
section before running anything there. Before solving a box problem, search `~/localrig`'s
`FINDINGS.md` and `TECHNICAL-FACTS.md`; most have already been measured.

## Access and the credential model

- SSH alias `ascent` (user `hslee1981`), configured on the Mac. GoverningDocs lives under
  `~/governingdocs/` on the box: `data/` (the code), `snapshots/` (training data), `runs/`.
- **HuggingFace models are always PRIVATE. Never create or publish a public model, dataset or Space under GoverningDocs** (they are trained on customer and licensed documents). Uploads from the box go through `scripts/release/`, which refuses a
  public repo (`ml/models/_common/hf_private.py`).
- **Credentials: scoped secrets only** ([#20](https://github.com/governingdocs/data/issues/20),
  revised 2026-10-01 from option A to B). The box holds a **read-only Doppler service token** for
  the separate project `governingdocs-spark` (config `prd`), which contains `HF_TOKEN` (upload
  trained models to the HuggingFace Hub), `BACKEND_READ_TOKEN` (a read-only GitHub token for
  governingdocs/backend: the release gate's backend checkout, `scripts/spark/setup_backend.sh`,
  and safe_export.py's lock check; added 2026-10-21), `OPENAI_API_KEY` (embeddings; added 2026-10-21)
  and `LLAMA_CLOUD_API_KEY` (LlamaParse). The last two make the box the place for paid-API scripts
  (Alex, 2026-10-27, [#204](https://github.com/governingdocs/data/issues/204)): `warehouse/parse/
  llamaparse_pages.py parse`, `production_parse.py` (its docstring has the run command) and
  `ml/models/ccr_binary_classifier/scripts/package_retrain.py embed`. Local models first still holds:
  paid runs are for production parity and benchmarks, each logs its page/credit/token counts, and a
  dry run comes first. Use spend-capped keys where the provider allows it. Nothing else is on the box: no write git, AWS or database secrets. The token lives in `~/.doppler/.doppler.yaml`
  (mode 0600, scoped to `~/governingdocs`); the eval agent's `evalagent` user cannot read
  `/home/hslee1981`. Jobs get it only when queued with `run_job.sh --secrets`.
  - Rotate or revoke: `doppler configs tokens --project governingdocs-spark --config prd` lists
    it (`spark-box`); `doppler configs tokens revoke spark-box --project governingdocs-spark
    --config prd` cuts the box off. Replace the HF token with
    `doppler secrets set HF_TOKEN --project governingdocs-spark --config prd`.
  - The current `HF_TOKEN` is a classic write token for the `hslee1981` account (all of its
    repos). Prefer a fine-grained token limited to the `GoverningDocs` org; swap it in with the
    command above.
  - The Doppler CLI is installed in `~/.local/bin` (no apt, no sudo).
- GoverningDocs may use the box for any training or fine-tuning (decided 2026-10-01).
- **Never poll the box from a Mac-side loop.** Every wait in these scripts runs box-side inside a
  single ssh session (`OPERATING.md`: 1,182 logins in 33 h came from Mac-side polling).

## One-time setup (done 2026-10-01)

```bash
scripts/spark/push.sh --snapshot governingdocs_data-20261001 --sync
scripts/spark/run_job.sh --name smoke --wait --snapshot governingdocs_data-20261001 -- \
    python scripts/spark/smoke_test.py
```

`--sync` runs `uv sync --frozen` on the box from the same `uv.lock` the Mac uses. On
linux-aarch64, `pyproject.toml` takes torch (>= 2.13, the first with sm_121 kernels) from the
PyTorch cu130 index; the Mac keeps PyPI's torch. The smoke test checks imports for all four model
stacks, a GPU training step, and sm_121 SASS in `libtorch_cuda.so` via `cuobjdump`
(`torch.cuda.get_arch_list()` under-reports on this box).

## The training loop

```bash
# 1. Push code (tracked files). The training data is the lake, already on the box.
scripts/spark/push.sh [--sync]                                          # --sync after uv.lock changes

# 2. Queue it on the GPU (runs behind the programme's numbered arms, one job at a time).
#    The page loaders read the lake, pinned to its current snapshot (recorded in run.json).
scripts/spark/run_job.sh --wait -- \
    python -m ml.models.xgboost_page_classifier.scripts.run_experiment
# Laya trainers checkpoint every 15 min and at epoch ends, resume on QR_RESUMED=1 or --resume:
scripts/spark/run_job.sh --resumable yes --name laya-page-classifier-train -- \
    doppler run -- python -m ml.models.laya_page_classifier.training.train \
    --epochs 3 --lr 2e-5 --device cuda --tf32 --eval-bs 4 \
    --out ml/models/laya_page_classifier/results/l1-finetune
# (same pattern for laya_ccr_binary_classifier, which still reads a legacy snapshot: --snapshot NAME)
# Reproduce a run on the data it read: --lake-snapshot <n> (from its run.json)

# 3. Bring artifacts and run records back.
scripts/spark/pull.sh

# Ship a model: train, upload a candidate from the box, gate it on the box; on PASS open a backend
# ticket for the pin bump (see ml/models/README.md, "Shipping a model to production"). Trains on
# the lake; the gate judges it on the lake's test split at the run's snapshot (heldout.py exports
# it). The gate needs the backend checkout and env on the box first (re-run after backend lock
# changes; idempotent) and the frozen package texts
# (ml/label_audit/package_eval_2026-10/package_texts.json, gitignored; S3 copy
# backups/release/package_texts_59c8a1dd.json):
ssh ascent 'cd ~/governingdocs/data && ~/.local/bin/doppler run -- scripts/spark/setup_backend.sh'
scripts/release/release.sh --model xgboost_page_classifier
```

### Data: the lake, and legacy DuckDB snapshots

By default a run reads the lake (#198): `job.sh` pins the lake's current snapshot when the job
starts, sets `GOVERNINGDOCS_PAGE_DATA=lake@<n>`, and records `lake@<n>` as the run's snapshot in
`run.json`. The page loaders (multilabel, XGBoost, Laya, COI) read it through
`warehouse/page_labels.py`, with the same training data as the legacy snapshot
(`scripts/spark/page_label_parity.py`; see `warehouse/README.md`). `--lake-snapshot <n>` pins an
earlier snapshot.

Scripts not yet on the lake (#204-#207) still take `--snapshot NAME`, a legacy DuckDB
snapshot. `governingdocs_data` is read-only since the #198 cutover (2026-10-19; its last write
was 2026-10-13), so `governingdocs_data-20261014-holdout` on the box is the last snapshot and
`export_snapshot.py` is gone (in the repository history). How they work:

The box has no Postgres. A snapshot is the training tables of `governingdocs_data` in one DuckDB
file plus `manifest.json` (row counts, sha256, source commit). On the box,
`job.sh` checks the sha256 and sets `GOVERNINGDOCS_DB_URL=duckdb:///...?access_mode=read_only`;
the model configs read that variable, so loaders and their SQL are unchanged. Verified: the v5.0
XGBoost split is identical from Postgres and from the snapshot (train 9,096, test 2,451, same row
order). Loader SQL must stay portable between Postgres and DuckDB (no `~*`, `::regclass` or other
Postgres-only syntax). They remain only until those scripts read the lake (#204-#207).

PDF corpora are not on the box yet; nothing that trains today needs them (the XGBoost, SetFit and
CCR loaders read text from the database). Push them when a parsing job needs them
([#23](https://github.com/governingdocs/data/issues/23)).

### Everything runs on the GPU

Every job goes through the box's GPU queue as `~/queue.d/gd-<run_id>.sh`: one job at a time,
inside the queue's 114 GB memory cgroup, after the programme's numbered arms. Training code uses
the GPU wherever it can: XGBoost sets `device="cuda"` when its build has CUDA (it does on the box;
the Mac's build stays on CPU), and models are saved back as CPU models because production serves
them on CPU. torch and sentence-transformers pick up CUDA by themselves. Don't hide the GPU
(`CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=""`) in training scripts.

**OCR runs on the GPU, never the CPU** (Alex, 2026-10-15). `warehouse/parse/ocr_pages.py` runs
Docling on CUDA with RapidOCR's PyTorch engine on CUDA (`RapidOcrOptions(backend="torch")`,
`EngineConfig.torch.use_cuda`), and stops if CUDA is missing. The CPU engine (ONNX Runtime) is
for small local smoke tests only (`--device cpu --limit N`). Why: the first OCR run used RapidOCR's
CPU engine on 6 workers, held every core and tripped the thermal watchdog (SoC 91 C, clock cut to
1800 MHz, queue halted). Any new OCR or other image-heavy job follows the same rule: put the work
on the GPU and keep CPU worker pools small.

The CPU work that remains (page rendering, image pre/post-processing) has two guards. Each worker
is held to `--threads` CPU threads (default 2; torch, OpenCV and BLAS would otherwise each start one
thread per core in every worker). And a CUDA run refuses to start outside `~/tools/cpu-job.sh`, the
box's CPU cap (400% = 4 cores' worth) with a thermal pause at 84 C, below the 90 C watchdog: queue it
with `scripts/spark/run_job.sh --cpu-quota 400% ...`. Workers are spawned, not forked, because the
parent loads the models on CUDA first and a forked child cannot use that CUDA context.

**Jobs that need no GPU** (lake queries, loads, exports) are queued with `run_job.sh --gpu none`.
The queued file then declares `# GPU: none`, and the box's queue runs it beside the training arm that

content.content:
The queued file then declares `# GPU: none`, and the box's queue runs it beside the training arm that
holds the GPU, in its own small sandbox (8 GB memory, 2 CPU cores' worth, `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`
empty), instead of pausing that arm. Why: on 2026-10-15 two `warehouse.lake --status` jobs (0 s of
work each) paused a 27B LoRA, and each pause cost about 9 minutes (1 to save, 8 to reload the
model). Never use it for a job that needs CUDA or more than 8 GB; such a job fails rather than
being given the GPU, and it is for hi jobs only and cannot be combined with `--cpu-quota`
(`run_job.sh` refuses both). **Not live yet:** the side lane and the load hold-off are in the staged
runner, which `~/tools/runner-side-test/install-side-runner.sh` installs at the next gap in the arms (deadline
2026-10-22); until then a `--gpu none` job still pauses the arm. Separately, the queue no longer pauses a training arm in its first 10 minutes
(its model load), so a GPU hi job that arrives then waits out the rest of the load.

A queued job must say what happens if the box reboots mid-run (`OPERATING.md`, "every queued arm
must be resumable"). **Every job we run (Alex, 2026-10-14) must:**

1. **Checkpoint:** write results as it goes (append and flush per batch or item; final files
   written to a temp name and renamed), and for training save model, optimizer, RNG and position
   in the epoch at least every 15 minutes (`train.py --ckpt-every-min`).
2. **Pause and resume at any point:** a kill (SIGTERM or SIGKILL) loses at most one interval; a
   restart, on `QR_RESUMED=1` or `--resume`, continues instead of starting over.
3. **Log progress about every minute:** done/total, rate, ETA, so a stalled job is visible.

`--resumable yes` is the default and declares exactly that. `--resumable restart-safe` (re-running
from the top) is only for jobs of a few minutes. GoverningDocs queue files are named `gd-...`, so
they sort after the programme's numbered arms (the runner logs a lexical-order warning for them;
that is expected).

### Run records

Every run writes `ml/models/<pkg>/evaluations/spark_runs/<run_id>/` on the box, and `pull.sh`
copies it back: `run.json` (command, rc, pushed commit and dirty-file count, snapshot name and
sha256, wall time, peak RSS, max SoC temperature), `freeze.txt` (`uv pip freeze`), `time.txt`,
`thermal.csv`, `log.txt`, and `artifacts.txt` (every file the run wrote). `pull.sh` copies new
files only, so it never overwrites local edits. `thermal.csv` stays out of git (`.gitignore`);
`run.json` keeps its peak.

### Watching

```bash
ssh ascent ./check-jobs.sh     # running jobs (includes GoverningDocs' spark/job.sh)
ssh ascent ./qstat.sh          # the GPU queue
```

## Services on the box

**The lake catalog (#195):** a user-space Postgres 18 (conda-forge via micromamba, no sudo, no apt)
that holds the DuckLake catalog, run as the `systemd --user` unit `governingdocs-lake-pg`
(`MemoryMax=2G`, restart on failure, enabled with linger, which `install` turns on, so it starts at boot). It listens on
`localhost:55432` and a socket in `~/governingdocs/lake/pg/run` only. Everything lives under
`~/governingdocs/lake/`: `pg/` (binaries, cluster, password file 0600), `data/` (Parquet),
`pdfs/` (`<sha256>.pdf`, #197) and `lake.env`, which exports the `GOVERNINGDOCS_LAKE_*` settings.

```bash
ssh ascent bash governingdocs/data/scripts/spark/lake_catalog.sh install   # idempotent
ssh ascent bash governingdocs/data/scripts/spark/lake_catalog.sh status    # unit, memory, restarts, lake
# warehouse.lake reads ~/governingdocs/lake/lake.env itself (over ssh and in queued jobs)
```

## Troubleshooting

All from `~/localrig/OPERATING.md`, where the incident behind each is recorded.

- **rc=137**: the kernel killed the job for memory (the queue's 114 GB cgroup), not a code failure.
- **rc=143 within a minute, `ORPHANED SCOPE` in `~/jobs/queue-stall-watchdog.log`**: the watchdog
  found no process running a `queue.d/*.sh` in the job's scope and SIGTERMed it. Queue files must
  never `exec` their payload (the 2026-10-01 first GPU run died this way); `run_job.sh` runs
  `job.sh` as a child for this reason.
- **`std::bad_alloc` or CUDA OOM with plenty of memory free**: stale page cache on the unified
  memory box. `ssh ascent sudo -n /usr/local/bin/drop-caches`.
- **Read-only filesystem after an unsafe shutdown**: see `OPERATING.md` before doing anything.
- **Never update the OS, driver or firmware** (and never press "Update" in the DGX Dashboard).
- Long GPU runs can still hit the box's unresolved multi-hour fragmentation freeze
  (`53-finetuning-case.md`); checkpoint them.

## Disk budget

The box has a 916 GB disk shared with the programme's model weights (299 GB free on 2026-10-01).
Keep GoverningDocs under about 60 GB: the environment (~15 GB with CUDA torch), snapshots (~0.3 GB
each; delete superseded ones after their runs are pulled), and model outputs.

# Models

Each subdirectory is a package that builds one of the platform's **current
production models** on [HuggingFace](https://huggingface.co/GoverningDocs). The repo
is kept to the code that builds (or is a build dependency of) a current model;
superseded exploratory experiments were removed (recoverable from git history).

> **Artifacts:** source, configs, findings docs, and small ground-truth / metrics
> files are tracked here. Trained weights and large datasets are not (see the root
> [`README.md`](../../README.md) and [`.gitignore`](../../.gitignore)); they live on
> HuggingFace / object storage and are retrained or pulled down.

## Index

| Package | Builds (HuggingFace) | Task | Approach |
|---------|----------------------|------|----------|
| [`meeting_boundary_detection`](meeting_boundary_detection/) | [`GoverningDocs/meeting-minutes-classifier`](https://huggingface.co/GoverningDocs/meeting-minutes-classifier) | Classify meeting pages (
| [`ccr_binary_classifier`](ccr_binary_classifier/) | [`GoverningDocs/ccr-binary-logreg`](https://huggingface.co/GoverningDocs/ccr-binary-logreg) | Is this a CCR (declaration of covenants) document? (
| [`xgboost_page_classifier`](xgboost_page_classifier/) | [`GoverningDocs/xgboost-page-classifier`](https://huggingface.co/GoverningDocs/xgboost-page-classifier) | Page-level category classification (
| [`citation_verifier`](citation_verifier/) | [`GoverningDocs/citation-verifier`](https://huggingface.co/GoverningDocs/citation-verifier) | Does a quoted source passage support a report claim? (NLI) |
| [`laya_page_classifier`](laya_page_classifier/) | [`GoverningDocs/laya-multilingual-page-classifier`](https://huggingface.co/GoverningDocs/laya-multilingual-page-classifier) (private) | Page-level c
| [`laya_ccr_binary_classifier`](laya_ccr_binary_classifier/) | [`GoverningDocs/laya-ccr-binary-classifier`](https://huggingface.co/GoverningDocs/laya-ccr-binary-classifier) (private) | Is this a CCR 
| [`coi_detector`](coi_detector/) | [`GoverningDocs/coi-detector`](https://huggingface.co/GoverningDocs/coi-detector) (private) | Certificate-of-insurance pages (`INSURANCE_LIABILITY_CERTIFICATE`), as
| [`multilabel_page_classifier`](multilabel_page_classifier/) | (build dependency) | Shared page-data loading layer (`data/load_data.py`) reused by `xgboost_page_classifier` | TF-IDF data prep; only `

Each package carries its own `README.md` / `RESULTS.md` / findings docs with
detailed metrics and conclusions. Start there.

## Running a model build

The packages are importable as `ml.models.*`. Run modules from the repo root with
`uv run` (which uses the locked environment):

```bash
uv run python -m warehouse.setup                                        # one-time: create the DB + schema
uv run python -m ml.models.xgboost_page_classifier.scripts.run_experiment
```

Each package's `config.py` centralizes its hyperparameters and in-repo paths. Training data
comes from lake releases, not local PDF folders (#209).

add='''## Addenda

### 2026-11-12, before any embedding was computed and before any label was read

Thresholds, the pair and unit definitions, the rubric, the cap, the cutoff rule and the
strict reading are unchanged. The primary model is unchanged: it stays
`jinaai/jina-embeddings-v2-base-code`. What this addendum fixes, all before the first
embedding exists:

- **Pins, including the code that runs.** The primary needs `trust_remote_code`, and its
  `auto_map` points at a second repository, `jinaai/jina-bert-v2-qk-post-norm`, so pinning the
  model repository alone would not pin what executes. Both are pinned by commit:
  `jinaai/jina-embeddings-v2-base-code` at `516f4baf13dec4ddddda8631e019b5737c8bc250` and
  `jinaai/jina-bert-v2-qk-post-norm` at `3baf9e3ac750e76e8edd3019170176884695fb94` (last
  modified 2024-05-07). The code repository holds two files, `modeling_bert.py` (2,312 lines)
  and `configuration_bert.py` (177 lines), and the harness records their sha256 and refuses to
  load if either differs. The files were read for imports and scanned for network, process,
  `eval`, `exec` and pickle use on 2026-11-12: they import only `torch`, `transformers`,
  `numpy` and the standard library, and the scan found none of those patterns. That is a scan
  and not a full audit, and it is stated as such.
- **Safetensors only.** The model repository also ships a pickle-based `pytorch_model.bin`.
  Loads pass `use_safetensors=True`, so no pickle is ever deserialised.
- **Library versions are pinned and recorded.** Remote modeling code written in 2024 can fail
  on a newer `transformers`. The versions of `transformers`, `torch` and `sentence-transformers`
  that load it are fixed by the canary and recorded in every manifest row. Models run offline
  after the first fetch.
- **Sensitivity arms, reported and never decisive.** The pre-registration names one sensitivity
  model; it is extended to five, each calibrated by the same equal-volume rule on its own
  similarities, none able to change the verdict:

  | Model | License | Revision |
  |---|---|---|
  | `jinaai/jina-code-embeddings-0.5b` (as pre-registered; bench only) | cc-by-nc-4.0 | `4db235132dafbe56a8b9c5f59b59795ecf58a4a7` |
  | `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B` | apache-2.0 | `97b0c614be4d77ee51c0cef4e5f07c00f9eb65b3` |
  | `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-8B` (the "would a much stronger embedder change the verdict" arm) | apache-2.0 | `1d8ad4ca9b3dd8059ad90a75d4983776a23d44af` |
  | `microsoft/unixcoder-base` (context 1,026 tokens, so long functions truncate; counts reported) | apache-2.0 | `5604afdc964f6c53782a6813140ade5216b99006` |
  | `BAAI/bge-code-v1` | apache-2.0 | `bd67852057c5d7ddcc7b8234d9d6c410117ed851` |

  Licences and revisions were read from the Hugging Face API on 2026-11-12. None of the five
  needs remote code. Every arm, the primary included, is run with no instruction prefix on
  either side and with the model's published pooling at the pinned revision, then
  L2-normalised. Two of them (the Qwen and bge-code families) are instruction-aware, so a null
  from them at this default is not evidence about instructed use.
- **Labeling budget for the arms.** The sensitivity pass labels at most 100 pairs per arm that
  are not already in the primary pool, drawn with seed 587 over pair ids alone before any
  packet is built. A pair two arms share is labeled once, and the pass is capped at 500 pairs
  in total. This replaces the single cap of 100 in "Sample".
- **Numerics.** All embeddings come from one CUDA GPU host with one fixed dtype (float32) and
  one fixed device, with batches ordered by token length then pair id. Vectors from different
  devices or dtypes are never merged: the cutoff is a threshold on cosine similarity, and
  mixed numerics can move a pair across it. The cache key gains the device, the dtype and the
  library versions. The results name the hardware only as "a single CUDA GPU host".
- **Pipeline split, no change to any definition.** Function texts are extracted on the
  analysis machine with archy's own parser and keyed by the sha256 of the normalised text. The
  embedding is a text-in, vectors-out job on the GPU host, with a manifest per shard. Top-1
  cosine, the cutoff and all scoring run on the analysis machine, from the returned vectors.
- **Bootstrap constants.** The PR-clustered bootstrap for pair precision uses 2,000 resamples
  and seed 587, as in `bench/embedding_oracle_stats.py` (#973). The remaining post-pilot
  quantities (M, the cutoffs, the capped A target) are still to be fixed in the post-pilot
  addendum.
- **A fine-tuned model is not part of this study.** Using one would need its own dated
  addendum before its weights are used, with training data disjoint from every repository in
  this study's sample and never the study's labels.
- **How the primary was kept.** It was pre-registered before anything ran, and keeping it
  makes this study carry no deviation in its primary instrument. The cost accepted is the
  remote-code pin above, and the canary still has to pass for it before any real run.

Adversarially review ONE dated addendum to a pre-registration, read-only. Do not edit files. No em dashes in your output.

File: /Users/hosanglee/archy/docs/research/EMBEDDING_ORACLE_RECALL.md. Review only the section "### 2026-11-12, before any embedding was computed and before any label was read" under "## Addenda" (the rest is the already-reviewed pre-registration; read it for context, and read the "Sample", "Cutoff" and "Thresholds" sections to check the addendum against them). The harness logic it refers to is in bench/embedding_oracle_pairs.py, bench/embedding_oracle_share.py, bench/embedding_oracle_score.py and bench/embedding_oracle_stats.py.

Try to find ways the addendum could produce a misleading result or an unfair claim, or contradict the pre-registration. Probe:
1. Five sensitivity arms plus the primary: does the labeling budget (100 pairs per arm outside the primary pool, 500 total, seed 587, shared pairs labeled once) interact badly with the 300-pair primary cap and the pooled-labeling blindness rule? Can a sensitivity arm's pairs leak into or contaminate the primary pool, the TRUE-pool floor, or the "only by B" share? Does the addendum say clearly that sensitivity arms never enter the headline share or the primary precision?
2. Multiple arms and forking paths: with five extra models reported in full, what stops a reader (or the author) from promoting whichever arm gives the best-looking number? Is "never decisive" operational enough, and what wording would close the gap?
3. The pin policy: is "refuses to load if either differs" enough for remote code (consider the model repo's own files, tokenizer files, the 'onnx' and 'pytorch_model.bin' siblings, transformers version drift, and the loader fetching other files)? Is a scan for network, process, eval, exec and pickle use fairly described as a scan?
4. Numerics: one device and dtype is fixed, but the addendum says the host is named only as "a single CUDA GPU host". Is the claim reproducible enough, and does it conflict with the pre-registration's requirement to record device, dtype and revisions?
5. 'No instruction prefix on either side' and 'published pooling': is this underspecified for any of the five models in a way that two people would implement differently?
6. Anything the addendum asserts that is not true or not supported (check the revisions are 40-hex, licences as stated, the line counts).

Report a ranked list: quote, failure scenario, severity (blocks merge / edit before merge / note), suggested wording. If an area is sound, say so in one line.

Padding side and EOS handling are set by the pinned tokenizer config and asserted by the canary."

- Wording: "Arm results are labeled `sensitivity`. No arm number appears in the verdict line, the abstract or the WHAT_DIDNT_WORK entry headline. A pass or kill is computed only from the primary arm. A reading such as 'an embedder at A's operating point works' needs a new pre-registration."

- Leak and pooling gaps:
  - Arm pairs are labeled after the primary 300 are drawn, so they cannot enter the primary pool, the TRUE-pool floor or the headline share. Say so explicitly.
  - The 100 per arm is "not already in the primary pool", but "primary pool" is ambiguous. It could mean the pre-draw pool (above 300) or only the 300 drawn. A pair in the pre-draw pool but outside the 300 would be a free arm pair or a leak into the labeled set.
  - "A pair two arms share is labeled once" does not say which arm's 100 slots it consumes.
  - 5 arms times 100 is 500, so the 500 total cap is a no-op unless sharing reduces it. State whether the cap binds and how.
  - When two arms share a pair, one label serves both. Say whether each arm's 100 are drawn independently and then unioned.
- The labeler blindness covers generator and arm identity, but shared packets could carry arm tags. Say they do not.
- Wording: "Arm pairs are drawn only from pairs outside the full pre-draw primary pool (A pairs, primary-B pairs and any sensitivity pairs), after the 300-pair primary draw is fixed. They never enter the headline share, the TRUE-pool floor or the primary precision. Each arm draws independently with `Random(587)` over sorted pair ids. The union is labeled once. Packets carry no arm tag."
- Also note that arm precision is measured over at most 100 pairs per arm, not a full labeled pool, so it is a weak estimate. The arm's "found by" figures cannot be computed on the arm's own pairs, and the addendum should say which arm statistics are reported.

- Quote: "the harness records their sha256 and refuses to load if either differs".
- Failure: the `jina-bert-v2-qk-post-norm` code is pinned and hashed, which covers its two `.py` files. It does not cover the tokenizer and config files, or the model repo's `config.json`. The model repo's `config.json` is the file that carries `auto_map`.
- Also uncovered:
  - `trust_remote_code` loaders fetch from the Hub at load time unless revision is passed for both repos. Passing `revision=` to the model repo does not, in all `transformers` versions, pin the repo referenced by `auto_map`. The reference is parsed as `repo--file`, and some versions default to `main`.
  - `bge-code-v1` ships `tokenization_qwen.py`, so the claim "None of the five needs remote code" is unverified for it. Its `config.json` has no `auto_map`, but its tokenizer config may. Either confirm and state it, or pin and hash that file too.
  - `jina-code-embeddings-0.5b` lacks `tokenizer_config.json` and `tokenizer.json`, so tokenizer loading is underspecified for that arm.
  - The model repos ship `onnx/` and `pytorch_model.bin` siblings. With `use_safetensors=True` they are ignored, but nothing says to restrict which files are downloaded.
- Wording: "Every load uses `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1` after a snapshot download of the pinned revision with an allow-list of file patterns. Every file in each snapshot, including config, tokenizer and `.py` files, is sha256-recorded, and the harness refuses to load if any file differs. For the primary, `auto_map` resolution is asserted to read the pinned code snapshot."
- Describing the scan as "a scan and not a full audit" is fair. The grep patterns should be named, and whether the scan covered both `.py` files should be stated. A scan of 2,312 lines for `eval`, `exec` and `pickle` will not catch indirect `importlib`, `getattr` or dynamic-loading paths. Add `importlib`, `__import__`, `subprocess`, `os.system`, `socket`, `urllib`, `requests` and `torch.load` to the named list.

**7. Edit before merge. The numerics claim is not reproducible as written, and it is in tension with the pre-registration.**
- Quote: "The results name the hardware only as 'a single CUDA GPU host'."
- Failure: the pre-registration says "the results quote the model id and revision that each cached vector row carries", and the addendum says the cache key gains device, dtype and library versions. Naming the hardware only as a generic phrase means a reader cannot tell which GPU or driver produced the vectors. The cutoff is a threshold on a similarity, so the GPU, CUDA version and TF32 flag matter.
- fp32 on a GPU is not deterministic by default. TF32 matmul, cuDNN autotuning and batch composition can change values at about 1e-6. With a hard threshold, pairs tied or near-tied at the cutoff can flip.
- The 8B model at fp32 needs about 32 GB of weights plus activations. State a minimum GPU memory.
- Wording: "The manifest records GPU model, driver and CUDA versions, `torch` version, `torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32=False`, `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms` setting and the batch size. The results quote these. 'A single CUDA GPU host' is the public description only." Also say that a cutoff computed on those vectors is applied only to vectors from the same host, and that the canary asserts the same pair order across two batch sizes.

**8. Note. "Sensitivity model gets its own cutoff" now means five calibrations.**
- Each arm calibrates its own cutoff on the 40-PR calibration subset. That subset is already small, and the cutoff is noisy.
- State that realised volume per arm is reported beside A's, and that an arm whose calibration cannot reach the target uses the lowest observed similarity (as the cutoff section already says).
- Also say that an arm with a very different score scale, such as UniXcoder, which has short context and truncates, does not make cutoffs comparable across arms.

**9. Note. A smaller wording issue in the claims.**
- "The primary is unchanged ... makes this study carry no deviation in its primary instrument." This holds for the model identity but not for the loading configuration. The `use_safetensors=True`, offline, pinned-library and no-prefix settings are new constraints that were not in the pre-registration. They are tightenings and are fine, but "no deviation" overstates it. Suggest: "no change of model, thresholds or rubric".
- "Last modified 2024-05-07" for the code repo is correct. The model repo itself was modified 2025-01-06, after the pre-registered check on 2026-10-28, so nothing in it changed since.

## Areas that are sound
- Revisions: all seven are 40-hex and equal to the API's current head.
- Licences: jina-code-embeddings-0.5b is cc-by-nc-4.0, bench-only, and the other four are apache-2.0.
- Threshold-side interaction: the verdict logic in `bench/embedding_oracle_score.py` reads only primary data, and the addendum leaves the thresholds, pair and unit definitions untouched.
- Pipeline split: the text-in, vectors-out job on the GPU host, with scoring on the analysis machine, changes no definition.
- Bootstrap constants match `bench/embedding_oracle_stats.py`.
- The fine-tuned-model exclusion is clear.</result>

content.thinking: Three of the five candidate models don't fit my rules: unixcoder-base ships only a .bin file, bge-code-v1 needs a remote tokenizer file, and UniXcoder has no pooling config. I'll correct all of that in one commit on #974.

input.command:
cd ~/archy; python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p='docs/research/EMBEDDING_ORACLE_RECALL.md'
s=open(p).read()
i=s.index('### 2026-11-12, before any embedding was computed')
add='''### 2026-11-12, before any embedding was computed and before any label was read

Thresholds, the pair and unit definitions, the rubric, the cap, the cutoff rule and the
strict reading are unchanged. The primary model is unchanged: it stays
`jinaai/jina-embeddings-v2-base-code`. This addendum makes no change of model, thresholds or
rubric; it adds loading constraints that the pre-registration did not state, all fixed before
the first embedding exists.

**Pins, including the code that runs**

- The primary needs `trust_remote_code`, and its `auto_map` points at a second repository,
  `jinaai/jina-bert-v2-qk-post-norm`, so pinning the model repository alone would not pin what
  executes. Both are pinned by commit: `jinaai/jina-embeddings-v2-base-code` at
  `516f4baf13dec4ddddda8631e019b5737c8bc250` and `jinaai/jina-bert-v2-qk-post-norm` at
  `3baf9e3ac750e76e8edd3019170176884695fb94` (last modified 2024-05-07).
- **Every file of every snapshot is hashed.** Each model is fetched once as a snapshot of its
  pinned revision with an allow-list of file patterns (weights, configs, tokenizer files and
  `.py` files; no `onnx/`), every file's sha256 is recorded, and every later load runs with
  `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1` and refuses if any file differs. For the primary, the harness asserts
  that the `auto_map` code resolves into the pinned code snapshot and not into `main`.
- **Remote code, stated exactly.** The primary needs the two files of its code repository
  (`modeling_bert.py`, 2,312 lines; `configuration_bert.py`, 177 lines). `BAAI/bge-code-v1`
  needs one in-repo tokenizer file, `tokenization_qwen.py`, named in its tokenizer config. The
  other four arms need none. Both remote files are pinned and hashed like any other.
- **What was scanned.** On 2026-11-12 the two code-repository files were read for imports and
  scanned for these patterns: `requests`, `urllib`, `socket`, `subprocess`, `os.system`,
  `eval(`, `exec(`, `pickle`, `__import__`, `importlib`, `open(`, `http`, `download`,
  `getenv`, `environ`. They import only `torch`, `transformers`, `numpy` and the standard
  library, and the only hit is the licence URL in a comment. That is a scan and not an audit;
  it does not catch indirect or dynamic loading. `tokenization_qwen.py` is scanned the same way
  before its first load, and a hit stops that arm.
- **Weights.** Loads pass `use_safetensors=True` for every model except
  `microsoft/unixcoder-base`, which ships only `pytorch_model.bin` at its pinned revision. That
  arm loads through the `weights_only` path with the file's sha256 pinned; if that path is
  unavailable the arm is dropped, never loaded with pickle deserialisation enabled.
- **Library versions** (`transformers`, `torch`, `sentence-transformers`) are fixed by the
  canary and recorded in every manifest row. Remote modeling code written in 2024 can fail on a
  newer `transformers`, and a version that loads it is part of the pin.

**Sensitivity arms, reported and never decisive**

The pre-registration names one sensitivity model; it is extended to five. Each is calibrated by
the same equal-volume rule on its own similarities.

| Model | License | Revision | Pooling |
|---|---|---|---|
| `jinaai/jina-code-embeddings-0.5b` (as pre-registered; bench only) | cc-by-nc-4.0 | `4db235132dafbe56a8b9c5f59b59795ecf58a4a7` | last token |
| `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B` | apache-2.0 | `97b0c614be4d77ee51c0cef4e5f07c00f9eb65b3` | last token |
| `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-8B` (the "would a much stronger embedder change the verdict" arm) | apache-2.0 | `1d8ad4ca9b3dd8059ad90a75d4983776a23d44af` | last token |
| `microsoft/unixcoder-base` (context 1,026 tokens, so long functions truncate; counts reported) | apache-2.0 | `5604afdc964f6c53782a6813140ade5216b99006` | mean over the attention mask |
| `BAAI/bge-code-v1` | apache-2.0 | `bd67852057c5d7ddcc7b8234d9d6c410117ed851` | last token |

The primary pools by mean, per its `1_Pooling` config. Pooling for the other models is the one
in their `1_Pooling` config at the pinned revision, except UniXcoder, which has none: mean over
the attention mask is chosen here and is this addendum's choice, not the model's published one.
Licences, revisions and pooling configs were read from the Hugging Face API on 2026-11-12.
Padding side and end-of-sequence handling come from the pinned tokenizer config, and the canary
asserts that a text embedded alone and inside a mixed batch gives the same vector to 1e-5.

- **No instruction prefix, made operational.** Texts are tokenized verbatim. `prompt_name=None`
  and `prompt=""` are passed explicitly, since the Qwen3, bge-code and jina-code configs ship
  prompt defaults, and the canary asserts that no prompt text appears in the tokenized input
  beyond the tokenizer's own special tokens. Two of the arms are instruction-aware, so a null
  from them at this default is not evidence about instructed use.
- **What an arm may and may not claim.** Arm results are labeled `sensitivity`. A pass or kill
  is computed only from the primary: no arm number appears in the verdict line, in the headline
  of the results or in the `docs/WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md` entry's headline, and no arm enters the
  headline share, the TRUE-pool floor or the primary precision. All six models are reported in
  one table, each with its interval. With six models reported in full, about one in six will
  look best by chance, and the study makes no claim that any non-primary arm would or would not
  pass. A kill is a kill for the primary at A's operating point. If a sensitivity arm would
  have cleared the bars, the results say so and recommend a new pre-registration instead of
  closing the line.
- **What an arm reports.** Its precision over its labeled pairs with an interval, its realised
  volume next to A's and the primary's, its truncation counts and whether its calibration
  reached the target. It reports no share and no verdict, since "found by" needs the full
  pooled labeling that only the primary gets. Cutoffs are not comparable across arms, since
  score scales differ.

**Labeling budget for the arms**

This replaces the cap of 100 pairs in the "Sensitivity model" bullet under "Generators"; the
primary's cap of 300 in "Sample" is unchanged and is drawn first.

- Arm pairs are drawn only after the primary draw is fixed, from pairs outside the full
  pre-draw primary pool (A's pairs and the primary's B pairs, whether or not the 300-pair draw
  kept them). They never enter the primary pool, the headline share, the TRUE-pool floor or the
  primary precision. An arm pair that is already in the labeled primary pool uses that label.
- Each arm draws at most 100 pairs independently with `random.Random(587)` over sorted pair
  ids. The union is labeled once under the same rubric and packet format, and packets carry no
  arm tag. Five arms of 100 is a ceiling of 500 only when no pair is shared; the cap binds only
  then.

**Numerics and what is recorded**

- All embeddings come from one CUDA GPU host with one fixed dtype (float32), TF32 matmul
  disabled, `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms` set and recorded, one fixed batch size, and
  batches ordered by token length then pair id. The 8B arm needs at least 48 GB of GPU memory
  at float32; if that is unavailable the arm is not run, not run at another dtype.
- Vectors from different devices, dtypes, batch sizes or library versions are never merged, and
  a cutoff is applied only to vectors from the configuration that calibrated it, because a
  threshold on similarity can flip a pair that mixed numerics move. The cache key gains the
  device, dtype, batch size and library versions, and the canary asserts the same pair order at
  two batch sizes.
- The results quote the model revisions, `torch` and `transformers` versions, CUDA version,
  dtype, the TF32 and determinism settings and the batch size. They describe the machine only
  as "a single CUDA GPU host" and do not name the GPU model, which a private manifest records.
  That withholds one reproducibility detail, and the results say so.

**Pipeline and the rest**

- Function texts are extracted on the analysis machine with archy's own parser and keyed by the
  sha256 of the normalised text. Embedding is a text-in, vectors-out job on the GPU host with a
  manifest per shard. Top-1 cosine, the cutoff and all scoring run on the analysis machine from
  the returned vectors. No definition changes.
- The PR-clustered bootstrap for pair precision uses 2,000 resamples and seed 587, as in
  `bench/embedding_oracle_stats.py` (#973). M, the cutoffs and the capped A target are still to
  be fixed in the post-pilot addendum.
- A fine-tuned model is not part of this study. Using one needs its own dated addendum before
  its weights are used, with training data disjoint from every repository in this study's
  sample and never the study's labels.
- **Why the primary stays.** It was pre-registered before anything ran, and keeping it means
  the study's instrument was not chosen after seeing anything. The cost accepted is the remote
  code above, and the canary still has to pass for it before any real run. The model repository
  was last modified on 2025-01-06 and the organisation's newer models are different families,
  so the pin is also the guarantee that it does not change under the study.
'''
open(p,'w').write(s[:i]+add)
PYEOF

content.text:
We're sticking with jina v2 as primary, and PR #974 (the addendum) now says so. CI is green on the fix commit `d2e491e6`, and #587 is still open.

**License.** The model repo declares Apache-2.0, so it's fine for research and for shipping later. The second repo whose code actually runs declares no license in its card, but its file headers carry the Apache-2.0 notice. I added that to the addendum. This is a factual read of the metadata, not a legal opinion.

**Is jina v2 still actively worked on?** No. The Jina organization is very active, with its v5 embedding models updated in October 2026, but `jina-embeddings-v2-base-code` was last modified 2025-01-06 and created 2023-11-17. It still gets about 142k downloads. For a pinned, offline study, no new commits is a feature, since the model can't change under the study. The cost is that it's an older model, so a null from it is a weaker statement than a null from a newer one. The addendum now says a kill is a kill for this primary at A's operating point. If a newer sensitivity arm would have cleared the bars, the results must say so and recommend a new pre-registration instead of closing the line.

**What the adversarial review changed in the addendum:**
- **Safetensors:** the rule can't hold for UniXcoder, which ships only `pytorch_model.bin`. That arm now loads through the `weights_only` path with the file hash pinned, or is dropped.
- **Remote code:** I had claimed none of the other models needed it. `bge-code-v1` ships a tokenizer file that is loaded as remote code, so it's now pinned and hashed like the primary's.
- **Pooling:** it's now listed per model. UniXcoder has no pooling config, so mean over the attention mask is chosen in the addendum and labeled as that.
- **Pins:** every file of every snapshot is hashed and loads run offline. The `auto_map` code must resolve into the pinned snapshot.
- **No prefix:** "no instruction prefix" is now enforced with explicit arguments and a canary check.
- **Arm results:** a sensitivity arm can't enter the verdict, the headline share, the TRUE-pool floor or the primary precision, and the addendum notes that with six models, one will look best by chance.
- **Arm labeling:** the budget cross-reference was wrong and is fixed. The draws are independent, packets carry no arm tag, and the 500-pair ceiling only binds if no pair is shared.
- **Numerics:** TF32 is off, determinism is set and recorded, and the 8B arm needs at least 48 GB of GPU memory or isn't run. The results will say "a single CUDA GPU host" and withhold the GPU model, and the addendum admits that withholds one reproducibility detail.

I haven't run a second review round on the revised addendum. The adversarial pass was round 1, and the DeepWork rules passed on the first version but not on `d2e491e6`. Want me to run round 2 before you merge, or hand it over now? Either way, stage 2 starts after the merge.

[2508.21290] Efficient Code Embeddings from Code Generation Models
Abstract:jina-code-embeddings is a novel code embedding model suite designed to retrieve code from natural language queries, perform technical question-answering, and identify semantically similar code snippets across programming languages. It makes innovative use of an autoregressive backbone pre-trained on both text and code, generating embeddings via last-token pooling. We outline the training recipe and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance despite the relatively small size of the models, validating this approach to code embedding model construction.

content.text:
Jina has released newer models, but none is a drop-in replacement for the primary, mainly because of licensing. I'd keep v2 as primary and change nothing in the addendum, unless you want one more sensitivity arm.

**What Jina has released since v2-base-code (2023-11):**

| Model | Released | License | Remote code | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `jina-code-embeddings-0.5b` / `1.5b` | Aug 2025 | cc-by-nc-4.0 | no | Built on Qwen2.5-Coder, last-token pooling, 32k context. The paper abstract says it can "identify semantically similar code snippets across programming languages", which is code-to-code, the closest match to Type-4 detection. |
| `jina-embeddings-v4` | May 2025 | Qwen Research License (non-commercial) | yes | 3.8B, has a `code` adapter. |
| `jina-embeddings-v5-text-small` / `nano` | Jan 2026 | cc-by-nc-4.0 | yes | General text models. The cards show no code-specific evidence. |
| `jina-embeddings-v5-omni-*` | Apr 2026 | cc-by-nc-4.0 | yes | Multimodal, so not relevant. |

**Every newer Jina model is non-commercial.** `jina-embeddings-v2-base-code` is the only Apache-2.0 Jina code model. The pre-registration chose it because it was the only candidate that could ship without a license problem, and that reason still holds.

If a newer Jina model wins, an archy tier couldn't ship it. You'd use an Apache-2.0 model like Qwen3-Embedding instead, or license Jina commercially. So the newer models are better as sensitivity arms ("how good can embeddings get") than as the primary.

**What I couldn't verify.** The paper says it is state-of-the-art for its size, but I read only the abstract. I haven't checked its numbers, and the cards give no head-to-head with v2-base-code.

**My recommendation.** The arm set already asks the "would a stronger embedder change the verdict" question through Qwen3-Embedding-8B, `bge-code-v1` and the pre-registered `jina-code-embeddings-0.5b`. I'd skip v4 and v5, since they need remote code, are non-commercial and are general-purpose.

The one optional addition is `jina-code-embeddings-1.5b`, the strongest Jina code model, as a sixth arm. It would cost one more model's embedding time, one more cutoff calibration and up to 100 more labeled pairs.

Should I add the 1.5b arm to the addendum, or leave it as is?

   - I re-ran the listed regex on `jina-bert-v2-qk-post-norm` at `3baf9e3a`. The line counts match (2,312 and 177), but there are 12 hits, not 1.
     - `modeling_bert.py` lines 10, 109, 683, 908, 922, 976, 979 and 1048: `http` in comments and docstrings.
     - `modeling_bert.py` line 1128: `self.eval()`, which matches the `eval(` pattern.
     - `configuration_bert.py` lines 10, 41, 78 and 80: `http` in comments and docstrings.
   - The imports also include `os`, `re`, `tqdm.autonotebook`, `tensorflow` (inside a function at line 105) and `optimum.exporters.onnx` (in `configuration_bert.py` at line 26). None of these is in the claimed list.
   - Scenario: a reader trusts a "clean" scan that was not clean. The `tokenization_qwen.py` rule, "a hit stops that arm", would also trip on any `http` comment.
   - Fix: "The scan produced 12 hits, all triaged by reading: `http` in comments and docstrings, and `self.eval()`, which is `nn.Module.eval`. Imports beyond torch, transformers, numpy and the standard library are `os`, `re`, `tqdm.autonotebook`, and `tensorflow` and `optimum` behind lazy or optional guards (modeling_bert.py:105, configuration_bert.py:26); `tensorflow` and `optimum` are not installed on the GPU host. For `tokenization_qwen.py`, a hit is read and triaged before the arm is stopped." The line about `tensorflow` and `optimum` being absent from the host is a statement about the host, which I did not check. The harness should assert it, or the sentence should say what was actually done.

2. **An arm "clearing the bars" is a verdict the arm cannot produce.**
   - Quote: "It reports no share and no verdict" versus "If a sensitivity arm would have cleared the bars, the results say so and recommend a new pre-registration."
   - The pass bar needs the 30% only-by-B share, which arms do not compute. An arm can at most clear the precision bar.
   - Scenario: a post-hoc read says "the 1.5b arm passed", and that recommendation becomes an arm-driven action, the thing "never decisive" forbids.
   - Fix: "If an arm's precision interval lies wholly above 0.60, the results note it as a hypothesis for a new pre-registration. It is not a pass, does not change the primary verdict, and the share is not computed."

3. **The arm draw is biased and one sentence is dead.**
   - Quote: "drawn only ... from pairs outside the full pre-draw primary pool" and "An arm pair that is already in the labeled primary pool uses that label."
   - The second sentence can never fire, because arm pairs are drawn from outside that pool.
   - The first creates a worse problem. Arm precision is measured only on pairs the primary and A did not emit. For arms that agree with the primary, that sample is made of the arm's unique, likely lower-precision pairs, yet the addendum compares it to the primary's precision "in one table".
   - Fix: delete the dead sentence, or draw from all arm candidates and reuse existing labels. If the exclusion stays, state: "arm precision is over arm-only pairs, excludes pairs shared with A or the primary, and is not comparable to the primary's precision."

4. **"Two of the arms are instruction-aware" is wrong.** Five arms are: jina-code 0.5b and 1.5b (both ship `*_query` and `*_document` prompts), Qwen3 0.6B and 8B (a "query" prompt), and bge-code-v1 (instruction-style usage). Separately, "the Qwen3, bge-code and jina-code configs ship prompt defaults" is not true of bge-code. Its `config_sentence_transformers.json` at the pin has `prompts: {}`. Fix: "five of the six arms are instruction-trained; bge-code ships no named prompts."

**Note**

5. Padding side is not in the tokenizer config for Qwen3, so it falls back to HF's default of right padding. `tokenizer_config.json` is absent at that path for the jina-code models. Last-token pooling depends on padding side, so "comes from the pinned tokenizer config" is unreliable. The mixed-batch canary would catch a wrong vector, but the addendum should state the explicit padding side (left) for the last-token models, rather than relying on the canary to find it.

6. `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms` on CUDA needs `CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG` set, or it raises. Record it with the other settings.

7. "Every file of every snapshot is hashed" conflicts with the allow-list, since `onnx/` is excluded. Say "every fetched file".

8. "The strongest Jina code model" for the 1.5b is an unverified claim. The Hugging Face API shows only the two jina-code sizes in this family, so say "the larger of the two".

9. Process step 4 still lists "the model revisions" for the post-pilot addendum. Add: "revisions are fixed by the 2026-11-12 addendum".

10. "One in seven will look best by chance" is the right idea, but the arms are correlated, so the estimate is approximate. Say "about".

- Arm count: six arms, seven models total, a 600-pair ceiling and "the other five need none" are all consistent. No stale "five" or "four" remains.
- Revisions and licences: all 40-hex revisions match the HF API for the eight repositories checked. Licences match, including cc-by-nc-4.0 for both jina-code models, apache-2.0 for the others, and none declared for the code repository. The last-modified dates 2024-05-07 and 2025-01-06 also match.
- Pooling: the `1_Pooling` configs match the table. Jina v2 is mean, all jina-code, Qwen and bge-code models are last token, and UniXcoder has none, which the addendum states.
- Safetensors: only UniXcoder lacks a safetensors file. The `auto_map` cross-repo pin is correct. `tokenization_qwen.py` is the bge-code tokenizer remote code, named correctly.
- Labeling-budget cross-reference: the "Sensitivity model" bullet under "Generators" holds the "at most 100 pairs" sentence.
- Primary verdict independence: the addendum keeps the primary's verdict, the headline share and the TRUE-pool and scorable floors away from arm numbers.
- Cache key: the cache-key extension is consistent with the body. The body never required recording the device, so withholding the GPU model contradicts nothing.
- Process timing: M and the cutoffs remain deferred, as step 4 says.
- Em dashes: none in the diff.</result>

**Pins, including the code that runs**

- The primary needs `trust_remote_code`, and its `auto_map` points at a second repository,
  `jinaai/jina-bert-v2-qk-post-norm`, so pinning the model repository alone would not pin what
  executes. Both are pinned by commit: `jinaai/jina-embeddings-v2-base-code` at
  `516f4baf13dec4ddddda8631e019b5737c8bc250` and `jinaai/jina-bert-v2-qk-post-norm` at
  `3baf9e3ac750e76e8edd3019170176884695fb94` (last modified 2024-05-07).
- **Every file of every snapshot is hashed.** Each model is fetched once as a snapshot of its
  pinned revision with an allow-list of file patterns (weights, configs, tokenizer files and
  `.py` files; no `onnx/`), every file's sha256 is recorded, and every later load runs with
  `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1` and refuses if any file differs. For the primary, the harness asserts
  that the `auto_map` code resolves into the pinned code snapshot and not into `main`.
- **Remote code, stated exactly.** The primary needs the two files of its code repository
  (`modeling_bert.py`, 2,312 lines; `configuration_bert.py`, 177 lines), whose card declares no
  license while the file headers carry the Apache-2.0 notice; the model repository declares
  apache-2.0. `BAAI/bge-code-v1`
  needs one in-repo tokenizer file, `tokenization_qwen.py`, named in its tokenizer config. The
  other five arms need none. Both remote files are pinned and hashed like any other.
- **What was scanned.** On 2026-11-12 the two code-repository files were read for imports and
  scanned for these patterns: `requests`, `urllib`, `socket`, `subprocess`, `os.system`,
  `eval(`, `exec(`, `pickle`, `__import__`, `importlib`, `open(`, `http`, `download`,
  `getenv`, `environ`. They import only `torch`, `transformers`, `numpy` and the standard
  library, and the only hit is the licence URL in a comment. That is a scan and not an audit;
  it does not catch indirect or dynamic loading. `tokenization_qwen.py` is scanned the same way
  before its first load, and a hit stops that arm.
- **Weights.** Loads pass `use_safetensors=True` for every model except
  `microsoft/unixcoder-base`, which ships only `pytorch_model.bin` at its pinned revision. That
  arm loads through the `weights_only` path with the file's sha256 pinned; if that path is
  unavailable the arm is dropped, never loaded with pickle deserialisation enabled.
- **Library versions** (`transformers`, `torch`, `sentence-transformers`) are fixed by the
  canary and recorded in every manifest row. Remote modeling code written in 2024 can fail on a
  newer `transformers`, and a version that loads it is part of the pin.

**Sensitivity arms, reported and never decisive**

The pre-registration names one sensitivity model; it is extended to six. Each is calibrated by
the same equal-volume rule on its own similarities.

| `BAAI/bge-code-v1` | apache-2.0 | `bd67852057c5d7ddcc7b8234d9d6c410117ed851` | last token |

The primary pools by mean, per its `1_Pooling` config. Pooling for the other models is the one
in their `1_Pooling` config at the pinned revision, except UniXcoder, which has none: mean over
the attention mask is chosen here and is this addendum's choice, not the model's published one.

content.text:
Addendum 1 is merged to `main` as `32d69f23`, and #587 is still open. This time I checked it right after the merge, and I kept closing keywords out of the commit messages.

**What merged:**
- **Primary:** jina v2 stays the primary comparison model. Its model repo and the second repo that holds its modeling code are both pinned by commit, every fetched file is hashed, and loads run offline.
- **Sensitivity arms:** six, none able to affect the verdict. They are `jina-code-embeddings-0.5b` and `1.5b`, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and 8B, UniXcoder and `bge-code-v1`.
- **Rules:** the addendum also fixes pooling per model, the labeling budget for the arms (at most 100 pairs per arm, 600 in total), the numerics, and the rule that a kill is a kill for the primary only.

**Reviews and CI.** CI was green on all 21 checks on the final commit, and both DeepWork rules passed on it. The adversarial review ran twice. Round 1 found a blocker (UniXcoder can't load as safetensors) plus several edits. Round 2 found three more things.

First, my claim about the scan of jina's modeling code was wrong. My first regex was defective, so the addendum's "only hit is the license URL" was false. I redid it with an AST read and rewrote the paragraph from that. The files have no network, process, `eval`, `open` or pickle use. They do have guarded optional imports of `tensorflow`, `tqdm` and `optimum`.

Second, the same read found a real runtime fetch: the model's `encode()` loads a tokenizer by `config._name_or_path`. If the harness loaded jina by repo id, that tokenizer would come from `main`, unpinned. The addendum now requires loading from the local pinned snapshot, never by repo id.

Third, the rest were wording, count and pooling fixes. I did not run a third adversarial pass on the final text.

**Next.** Stage 2:
1. A Mac-side extractor writes function texts, keyed by the sha256 of the normalized text.
2. I push them to the GPU box and run the embedding job under governingdocs/data #572, loading jina from the local pinned snapshot, offline.
3. The vectors come back for scoring on the Mac.

The job also needs the canary to pass first, since a loop and a comprehension computing the same thing must embed closer than two unrelated functions. Should I start with the extractor?

**pre-registered expectation** and a **decision rule written before the run**, because this project
has three times produced a number and then argued about what it meant.

---

| rule | what it cost to learn |
|---|---|

| 🔴 **VALIDITY BEFORE SCORING** | `116` was blind-judged **3/3 on a treatment that was never applied** — `bakeoff.py` deleted the staged worktree. **A blind judge cannot see an absent treatment** |
| 🔴 **Judge within one round, re-judge the control in-round** | rubric-v1 scores do not compare across rounds. ✅ Reproduced exactly twice (`briefing-20260902`, `117b`) |
| 🔴 **Never compare a depth-loaded number to a depth-0 one** | Made **three times in three days** — GLM's MoE-vs-dense bandwidth, its 6.6-vs-17.71 t/s, and the B70's `p512/g128` headline |
| 🔴 **One session per file; never a pooled archive** | `65` pooled ~56 sessions per card (its 30-45% figure is an upper bound). `119`'s own guard read a **pooled** transcript dir and would have voided a clean control |
| 🔴 **Discovery ≠ capability** | Four pushes returned **0 of 89, 0 of 24, 0 of 38**, and the fifth (`111`) was **negative**. Before proposing a feature, check whether archy already answers it |

| ⚠️ **Pre-register the expectation, and report a null as plainly as a hit** | `117b` was pre-registered 3/3/3, landed 3/3/3, and killed [`72`](72-what-makes-a-card-discriminate.md) §3 — which is a result, not a wasted arm |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| **E2** | Is the payload wrong rather than the channel? | same channel, **crux** instead of symbol lists | ~10.5 h | 🔴 **DONE — NULL.** 1.128x (vs E1's 1.263x); a 3.7x smaller, content-shaped payload still did not cross 1.0. [scores](judge-bundles/crux-ab-202
| **E3** | Does the model reach for archy when it is merely AVAILABLE? | **PULL arm** — tools present, nothing injected | ~7 h | ⬜ never run |

| **E5** | How does Qwen3.8-27B decode at depth here? | `llama-bench -d 0,16384,65536,131072`, baseline tree | ~15 min | ⬜ owed; free during the meter session |
| **E6** | What does this box actually draw at the wall? | external meter, 4 paired states | ~1 h, no GPU | ⬜ hardware in hand |
| **E7** | Can 32 GB hold Qwen3.8-27B + 126K of KV? | desk analysis of published vLLM configs | ~1 h, no GPU | ⬜ owed |
| **E8** | What makes a card discriminate? | open design problem | — | 🔴 **reopened** by `117b` |
| **E9** | Is `65`'s re-derivation figure inflated by pooling? | re-stage one session per file, count within-session | ~2 h, no GPU | ⬜ owed |
| **E10** | Do our cost claims survive cache-aware accounting? | re-score push arms weighting injected prefill | ~1 h, no GPU | ✅ **DONE — both conclusions survive.** `111` brief 0.494x eval → **0.541x weighted**; `119` headers 1.263x → **1.282x weighted**. 🥇 
| **E11** | Phase 3 | the keep-or-return blocker | large | ⬜ **the only decision-blocking item** |

That was my design choice, not a hard requirement. The ticket doesn't mean "the agent can't touch it". The agent works on the Mac either way, since `~/localrig` lives there. The split is only about where the code executes, and I put the archy-side half on the Mac for four reasons.

1. **The inputs are already there.** The extractor needs checkouts of each PR's base and head commits, plus archy's parser. The #548 clones, the measured-PR ledgers (`bench/diff_duplicates_data/`) and the gitignored caches all live in `~/archy` on the Mac. On the box I'd have to push clones up first. #548 cost about 54 s per PR including cold clones, so the cloning dominates and the embedding doesn't.

2. **The box is the wrong place for CPU-heavy git work.** Its rules cap CPU jobs at about 400% with a thermal pause. A job that pushes cores hard once tripped the thermal watchdog and halted the queue. Its GoverningDocs disk budget is about 60 GB, and clones of many repos eat that quickly. Extraction is parsing and `git`, with no GPU use. Only the embedding step benefits from the GPU, so only that step goes there.

3. **The dev loop for a public repo lives on the Mac.** That repo's CI gates, `uv` environment, `gh` auth and DeepWork review all run from there. The box holds only scoped secrets and no write git access, so PRs can't originate from it.

4. **It keeps the private box out of the public repo.** If the code that writes archy PRs never runs on the box, there's less chance a hostname, path or log line leaks into a commit or result. The boundary is simple: function text goes out, vectors come back.

Nothing breaks if you'd rather run extraction on the box. It would need the repos pushed up, a low CPU quota and the thermal pause. Entry 300's design would change so the extractor sits in 299.

# DeepWork Review

Run automated code reviews on the current branch based on `.deepreview` config files.

## Routing — Check Before Proceeding

**STOP and redirect** if either of these applies:

- User wants to **configure, create, or modify** review rules (e.g., "add a security review", "set up reviews for our API layer") → use the `configure_reviews` skill instead
- User wants to **add a doc-sync rule** (keep a documentation file in sync with source files) → call `start_workflow` with `job_name="deepwork_reviews"` and `workflow_name="add_document_update_rule"`

Only proceed past this section if the user wants to **run** reviews.

## Pre-flight — Verify Agent Availability

Before running reviews, check that the `deepwork:reviewer` agent is available. If it does not appear in the agents list (i.e., the Agent tool does not list `deepwork:reviewer` as a valid `subagent_type`), **STOP** and tell the user:

> The `deepwork:reviewer` agent is not available. Please run `/reload-plugins` to pick up the latest plugin updates, then try again.

Do not proceed with reviews until the agent is available.

## How to Run

1. Call the `mcp__deepwork__get_review_instructions` tool directly:
   - **No arguments** to review the current branch's changes (auto-detects via git diff against the main branch).
   - **With `files`** to review only specific files: `mcp__deepwork__get_review_instructions(files=["src/app.py", "src/lib.py"])`. When provided, only reviews whose include/exclude patterns match the given files will be returned. Use this when the user asks to review a particular file or set of files rather than the whole branch.
   - **If the result says no rules are configured**: Ask the user if they'd like to auto-discover and set up rules. If yes, invoke the `/deepwork` skill with the `deepwork_reviews` job's `discover_rules` workflow. Stop here — do not proceed with running reviews if there are no rules.
2. The output will list review tasks to invoke in parallel. Each task has `description`, `subagent_type`, and `prompt` fields — these map directly to the Agent tool parameters. Launch all of them as parallel agents.
3. **While review agents run**, check for a changelog and open PR (see below).
4. Collect the results from all review agents.

## Changelog & PR Description Check

Run this concurrently with the review agents (step 2 above) — don't wait for reviews to finish first.

1. Check if the project has a changelog file (e.g., `CHANGELOG.md`, `CHANGELOG`, `CHANGES.md`).
2. If a changelog exists and there are commits on the current branch beyond the main branch:
   - Read the changelog and the branch's commit log (`git log main..HEAD --oneline`).
   - Verify the changelog's unreleased/current section accurately reflects what the branch does. If entries are missing, outdated, or inaccurate, update the changelog.
3. If a PR is open for the current branch (check with `gh pr view`):
   - If you updated the changelog, also verify the PR description matches. Update it with `gh pr edit` if needed.
   - If the changelog was already accurate, skip the PR description check.

## Acting on Results

For each finding from the review agents:

- **Obviously good changes with no downsides** (e.g., fixing a typo, removing an unused import, adding a missing null check): make the change immediately without asking. When in doubt, ask.
- **Everything else** (refactors, style changes, architectural suggestions, anything with trade-offs):
  1. Use AskUserQuestion to ask the user about each finding **individually**. Do not group issues together unless they are the same issue occurring in multiple files; otherwise, use AskUserQuestion to ask about each issue separately. This lets the user make separate decisions on each item.
  2. For each question, provide several concrete fix approaches as options when there are reasonable alternatives (e.g., "Update the spec to match the code" vs "Update the code to match the spec" vs "Skip").
  3. If a finding seems minor or debatable, include an option to suppress that error in the future — such as a clarification to the rule if it is too narrow, or a comment on the offending content if comments work in that context.
  4. Be concise — quote the key finding, don't dump the full review.

When a finding is dismissed (user chooses "Skip" or you determine it's not actionable for this PR), call `mcp__deepwork__mark_review_as_passed` with the review's ID so it won't re-run on subsequent iterations.

## Iterate

After making any changes:

1. Call `mcp__deepwork__get_review_instructions` with `files` set to **only the files you edited** during this iteration. This scopes the re-review to your changes rather than re-reviewing the entire branch.
2. Repeat the cycle (run → act on results → run again) until a clean run — one where all review agents return no findings, or all remaining findings have been explicitly skipped by the user.
3. On subsequent runs, you only need to re-run tasks that had findings last time — skip tasks that were clean.
4. Reviews that already passed are automatically skipped as long as reviewed files remain unchanged.

- The pilot is re-extracted, not read from the ledger, and its drop classes are compared with #548's: 7 measured, 9 no added Python lines, 4 `QualnameCollisionError`, 0 mismatches. A mismatch exits 3.

| shard | PRs in | PRs shipping | unique texts |
|---|---|---|---|
| pilot | 20 | 3 | 8,997 |
| calibration | 40 | 19 | 22,190 |

input.description: Adversarial review of PR 975 extractor
input.prompt:
Adversarially review a pull request, read-only. Do not edit, commit, check out, or switch branches in /Users/hosanglee/archy (another process may be using that checkout; the PR branch alee/emb587-extractor is already checked out there, so read files in place). No em dashes in your output.

PR: hslee16/archy #975, "bench: function-text extractor and shard writer for the #587 embedding oracle". New files: bench/embedding_oracle_extract.py, bench/embedding_oracle_extract_mutants.py, tests/test_embedding_oracle_extract.py. Use `git diff main...HEAD` and read the files in full.

Context to read first: the pre-registration and its addendum at docs/research/EMBEDDING_ORACLE_RECALL.md (sections Population and sampling, Generators, Cutoff, Pool and labeling, Process, and the Addenda), the #548 harness in bench/diff_duplicates_precision.py and bench/diff_duplicates_run.py and bench/diff_duplicates_pr.py, the pilot ledger bench/diff_duplicates_pilot.jsonl, the #548 measured-PR ledgers bench/diff_duplicates_data/precision.*.jsonl, and the stage-1 logic bench/embedding_oracle_pairs.py.

Your job is to find ways this extractor could silently corrupt the study's measurement before any model runs. Probe, in addition to anything you find:
1. DRAWS: are the pilot (the 20 PRs of #548's pilot) and the calibration subset (40 measured PRs, random.Random(587) over sorted PR keys, at most 5 per repository, drawn FIRST) implemented exactly as the pre-registration says, including the key being sorted, the per-repo cap being applied in draw order, and the calibration set being disjoint from the pilot? Can the evaluation subset be named or leaked from the CLI or by any code path? Is the "measured PR" set the one from #548's main ledgers and not re-derived differently?
2. WHICH FUNCTIONS: added-side = functions whose def line falls in an added hunk of merge-base(base, head)..head; base-side = functions that existed at base outside the added hunks, with the 30-node floor and source-only filter (test and vendored paths dropped). Compare against bench/diff_duplicates_precision.py's added-hunk logic and archy's own extraction. Look for off-by-one on hunk ranges, decorated defs (def line vs decorator line), nested and async defs, methods, renamed or moved files, deleted functions, functions present at base but modified by the PR (are they 'outside the added hunks' by line or by identity?), and the 'exists at base AND head' requirement stated in the addendum for B's neighbours: is it enforceable from what the extractor writes (does the per-PR index carry enough to check head existence)?
3. NORMALISATION AND KEYS: normalise() is line endings to LF and trailing newlines cut. Is the sha256 key stable across platforms, encodings, BOMs, tabs, trailing whitespace on lines, and Windows paths? Can two distinct functions collide on one id in a way that loses a (PR, function) mapping? Does dedupe across PRs ever drop a per-PR index row? Do shards stay deterministic (sorted, unique) across runs and PYTHONHASHSEED values?
4. DROPS AND LEDGER: unmeasurable PRs must be dropped with a reason and never scored clean, and the pilot drop classes must match #548's (7 measured, 9 no added Python lines, 4 QualnameCollisionError). Does the exit-3 mismatch check really compare per-PR classes or only counts? Is checkpoint and resume handled as AGENTS.md requires (one ledger row per unit appended in one write, only status ok counts as done, a crash in one PR does not end the loop, stalls retried and results never)? Is there any case where an interrupted run leaves a torn shard that a later run trusts?
5. SECRETS AND PRIVACY: nothing in the three files, their comments, docstrings, test names, paths or strings may mention the user's private GPU host or its tooling: grep for dgx, spark, gx10, ascent, gb10, localrig, ascent, doppler, and any hostname. Also check the PR body and commit message for a closing keyword (fix, fixes, close, closes, resolve) directly before an issue number.
6. TESTS: are the 21 tests and 18 mutants real? For three mutants of your choosing, actually reason about whether a test would turn red; flag any fixture that never reaches the branch it claims to test, and any test that asserts agreement between two things sharing an implementation instead of a hand-worked answer. Check the mutants script exits non-zero when a match is missing (read it).
7. Anything the PR body claims that the code does not do (check the shard counts claim of 3 of 20 pilot PRs shipping and 19 of 40 calibration PRs shipping against what the code would produce, and the claim that drops stay in the denominator).

Report a ranked list: file:line, quote, concrete failure scenario (inputs to wrong measurement), severity (blocks merge / edit before merge / note), suggested fix. One line per area that is sound.

Adversarially review a pull request, read-only. Do not edit, commit, check out, or switch branches in /Users/hosanglee/archy (another process may be using that checkout; the PR branch alee/emb587-extractor is already checked out there, so read files in place). No em dashes in your output.

PR: hslee16/archy #975, "bench: function-text extractor and shard writer for the #587 embedding oracle". New files: bench/embedding_oracle_extract.py, bench/embedding_oracle_extract_mutants.py, tests/test_embedding_oracle_extract.py. Use `git diff main...HEAD` and read the files in full.

Context to read first: the pre-registration and its addendum at docs/research/EMBEDDING_ORACLE_RECALL.md (sections Population and sampling, Generators, Cutoff, Pool and labeling, Process, and the Addenda), the #548 harness in bench/diff_duplicates_precision.py and bench/diff_duplicates_run.py and bench/diff_duplicates_pr.py, the pilot ledger bench/diff_duplicates_pilot.jsonl, the #548 measured-PR ledgers bench/diff_duplicates_data/precision.*.jsonl, and the stage-1 logic bench/embedding_oracle_pairs.py.

Your job is to find ways this extractor could silently corrupt the study's measurement before any model runs. Probe, in addition to anything you find:
1. DRAWS: are the pilot (the 20 PRs of #548's pilot) and the calibration subset (40 measured PRs, random.Random(587) over sorted PR keys, at most 5 per repository, drawn FIRST) implemented exactly as the pre-registration says, including the key being sorted, the per-repo cap being applied in draw order, and the calibration set being disjoint from the pilot? Can the evaluation subset be named or leaked from the CLI or by any code path? Is the "measured PR" set the one from #548's main ledgers and not re-derived differently?
2. WHICH FUNCTIONS: added-side = functions whose def line falls in an added hunk of merge-base(base, head)..head; base-side = functions that existed at base outside the added hunks, with the 30-node floor and source-only filter (test and vendored paths dropped). Compare against bench/diff_duplicates_precision.py's added-hunk logic and archy's own extraction. Look for off-by-one on hunk ranges, decorated defs (def line vs decorator line), nested and async defs, methods, renamed or moved files, deleted functions, functions present at base but modified by the PR (are they 'outside the added hunks' by line or by identity?), and the 'exists at base AND head' requirement stated in the addendum for B's neighbours: is it enforceable from what the extractor writes (does the per-PR index carry enough to check head existence)?
3. NORMALISATION AND KEYS: normalise() is line endings to LF and trailing newlines cut. Is the sha256 key stable across platforms, encodings, BOMs, tabs, trailing whitespace on lines, and Windows paths? Can two distinct functions collide on one id in a way that loses a (PR, function) mapping? Does dedupe across PRs ever drop a per-PR index row? Do shards stay deterministic (sorted, unique) across runs and PYTHONHASHSEED values?
4. DROPS AND LEDGER: unmeasurable PRs must be dropped with a reason and never scored clean, and the pilot drop classes must match #548's (7 measured, 9 no added Python lines, 4 QualnameCollisionError). Does the exit-3 mismatch check really compare per-PR classes or only counts? Is checkpoint and resume handled as AGENTS.md requires (one ledger row per unit appended in one write, only status ok counts as done, a crash in one PR does not end the loop, stalls retried and results never)? Is there any case where an interrupted run leaves a torn shard that a later run trusts?
5. SECRETS AND PRIVACY: nothing in the three files, their comments, docstrings, test names, paths or strings may mention the user's private GPU host or its tooling: grep for dgx, spark, gx10, ascent, gb10, localrig, ascent, doppler, and any hostname. Also check the PR body and commit message for a closing keyword (fix, fixes, close, closes, resolve) directly before an issue number.
6. TESTS: are the 21 tests and 18 mutants real? For three mutants of your choosing, actually reason about whether a test would turn red; flag any fixture that never reaches the branch it claims to test, and any test that asserts agreement between two things sharing an implementation instead of a hand-worked answer. Check the mutants script exits non-zero when a match is missing (read it).
7. Anything the PR body claims that the code does not do (check the shard counts claim of 3 of 20 pilot PRs shipping and 19 of 40 calibration PRs shipping against what the code would produce, and the claim that drops stay in the denominator).

Report a ranked list: file:line, quote, concrete failure scenario (inputs to wrong measurement), severity (blocks merge / edit before merge / note), suggested fix. One line per area that is sound.

**5. Writes are not atomic.**

- Fix: write to a temp file and `os.replace`. Make `main` write the manifest only after both audits pass.
